node.label: Charles Taylor
node.date_label: Sources of the Self: The Making of the Modern Identity (1989) · The Malaise of Modernity: CBC Massey Lectures (1991) · Multiculturalism and “The Politics of Recognition” (1992) · Multiculturalism: expanded edition with Taylor’s recognition essay (1994) · Modern Social Imaginaries: 2004 bibliographic edition (2004) · A Secular Age (2007) · Cosmic Connections: Poetry in the Age of Disenchantment (2024)
node.description: Examines the moral languages through which people understand themselves and their relations with others. In the selected Politics of Recognition passages, identity develops through dialogue rather than solitary self-creation; recognition can support or damage that development. Taylor distinguishes equal human dignity from a demand that every cultural product receive an identical evaluation. Comparative inquiry should remain open to changing its own standards. His later interview on Romantic poetry describes changes in experiences of cosmic order and argues that poetry can disclose forms of meaning without settling their metaphysical truth. These are situated philosophical arguments about modern identity and historical change, with their Western scope and normative commitments made explicit.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Sources of the Self (1989); The Malaise of Modernity (1991); “The Politics of Recognition” (1992; selected 1994 expanded-volume text); Modern Social Imaginaries (copyright 2004); A Secular Age (2007); Cosmic Connections (2024).
node.scope_note: The philosophical resources concern dialogical identity, cultural comparison and historically changing moral meanings. Selected essay passages and the complete displayed 2024 interview support the argument claims; the complete monographs remain unread. Amy Gutmann’s editorship and other commentators’ authorship are distinct from Taylor’s essay. No Canadian journalist or other Charles Taylor identity is included.

people_update.label: Charles Taylor
people_update.identity_note: Charles Taylor, the McGill philosopher born in Montreal in 1931, identified through his institutional bibliography, own essay and Wissenschaftskolleg report. Distinct from the journalist who wrote Radical Tories and from other Charles Taylors. No QID assigned or raw author-key merge.

proposed_edges.relationship: Explains identity as dialogically formed, making recognition and misrecognition consequential for human agency.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected primary printed pp. 25–37, especially 32–37. His historical narrative and normative claims remain his argument; this does not establish an invariant experience or one shared position of all identity historians.

proposed_edges.relationship: Requires comparative cultural inquiry to reconsider its own standards rather than predetermine equal evaluations of every cultural product.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected primary printed pp. 68–73. Equal dignity and openness to cultural value are distinguished from compulsory identical judgments. Taylor’s polemic against subjectivism is not adopted as a neutral description of Foucault, Derrida or multiculturalism as a whole.

proposed_edges.relationship: Investigates changing moral meanings through Romantic poetry’s responses to disenchantment and experiences of cosmic order.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own answers in the complete 2024 interview on historical cosmic orders, epistemic retreat and constitutive language. This is a philosophical resource for intellectual history; the full monograph and cited poets’ works remain unread.
